missing_spec_content.spec_text: running ~ 3 m/s ... Students should be able to recall typical values of speed for a person walking, running and cycling
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives typical speeds for walking, cycling, a car, sound and light. It never gives a typical running speed (keyPoints[1].content, keyPoints[1].writeBullets, revisionCardBullets).

missing_spec_content.spec_text: The speed of a moving object is rarely constant... The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on many factors including: age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not say that real speeds are rarely constant. It does not name the factors that affect how fast a person walks, runs or cycles.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: It is not only moving objects that have varying speed. The speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives one fixed value for the speed of sound. It never says that the speed of sound or the speed of the wind varies.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to make measurements of distance and time and then calculate speeds of objects.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not explain how to measure distance and time in order to work out a speed.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) Students should be able to explain qualitatively, with examples, that motion in a circle involves constant speed but changing velocity.
missing_spec_content.why: Circular motion (constant speed but changing velocity) is not covered anywhere in the lesson.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time can be determined by drawing a tangent and measuring the gradient of the distance–time graph at that time.
missing_spec_content.why: keyPoints[1].content says only that 'A curved line means the speed is changing'. It never teaches drawing a tangent to find the speed at one instant.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to draw distance–time graphs from measurements and extract and interpret lines and slopes of distance–time graphs
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson teaches how to read distance–time graphs but not how to draw one from measurements.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Students should be able to estimate the magnitude of everyday accelerations.
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson gives no typical everyday accelerations and no practice in estimating them.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: (HT only) measure, when appropriate, the area under a velocity–time graph by counting squares.
missing_spec_content.why: keyPoints[2].content teaches only triangle and trapezium areas. Counting squares, which is needed for curved graphs, is never mentioned.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: draw velocity–time graphs from measurements and interpret lines and slopes to determine acceleration
missing_spec_content.why: The lesson does not teach how to draw a velocity–time graph from measurements.

missing_spec_content.spec_text: Investigation to measure the effect of air resistance on a falling object eg a model parachute.
missing_spec_content.why: The suggested investigation into air resistance on a falling object is not mentioned.

above_gcse.text:
• v = u + at
• s = ½(u + v)t
above_gcse.why: These sections give only a = Δv/t and v² − u² = 2as. These two extra equations are not in the specification text.

above_gcse.text: SUVAT: The five motion quantities: displacement, initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration, time
above_gcse.why: 'SUVAT' is an A-level way of organising these equations and is not a specification term. Putting it at the centre of the key point suggests the student must use a full set of equations they are not required to know.
s = ½at² is not in the specification. It is not taught anywhere in the lesson either.

factual_errors.correction: North-east means 45°. The actual direction is about 53° north of east (bearing about 037°), because tan⁻¹(400/300) ≈ 53°. The specification requires the student to 'express a displacement in terms of both the magnitude and direction', so the direction should be stated correctly.

factual_errors.text: speed of sound in air ≈ 340 m/s
factual_errors.correction: The specification states 'A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s.' 340 m/s is a reasonable real-world value, but the lesson should give the specification value of 330 m/s. The same applies to the speed of sound value in keyPoints[1].writeBullets and revisionCardBullets.

wrong_terms.text: Equation: v = d/t. Rearrangements: d = vt, t = d/v.
wrong_terms.spec_term: s = v t (distance, s, in metres)
distance, s, in metres, m (in v² − u² = 2 a s)

wrong_terms.text: The net force and the acceleration both decrease.
Parachute opens. Drag increases hugely, so the net force is now upward.
T for Two forces balanced (weight = drag). No net force → no acceleration.

wrong_terms.spec_term: a = (∆ v)/t (acceleration = change in velocity / time taken)

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: checkpoints.4: A ball is dropped from rest and falls freely under gravity (g = 9.8 m/s²) for 3s. How far does it fall?
checkpoint_mismatch.key_point: keyPoints[4]: Terminal velocity and non-uniform acceleration
checkpoint_mismatch.why: Key point 4 is about uniform and non-uniform acceleration, free fall and terminal velocity. It gives no method for working out distance fallen. The question actually tests the equations in keyPoints[3]. The correctFeedback also uses s = ½at², which the lesson never teaches. Nothing about terminal velocity is tested.

checkpoint_mismatch.checkpoint: checkpoints.3: A motorcycle accelerates from 5 m/s to 25 m/s in 4s. What is its acceleration?
checkpoint_mismatch.why: The question is answered with a = (v − u)/t from keyPoints[2], as the feedback shows. It does not test choosing or using the equations of motion in keyPoints[3], such as v² = u² + 2as.

not_checked: All keyPoints have "diagram": null, so no diagrams were provided. Graph shapes (for example the skydiver velocity–time graph) are described only in words and could not be checked against a drawn graph.

Claims about exam frequency and mark values could not be checked, for example tutor_note 'Gradient calculations on d-t graphs come up almost every year', 'come up as 6-mark questions' and 'a very common 4-mark question'.
It is assumed that checkpoint keys '0' to '5' match keyPoints[0] to keyPoints[5] by index. The lesson JSON does not state this mapping.
